gd.enable_tbl_preview(n_head=8, n_tail=3)

Whether a network holds together, and how firmly, is one of the first things to ask of it. Can
every node reach every other? Which single node or link, if it failed, would cut the network in
two? How many independent routes join two places, and how much can flow between them at once? This
page covers the methods that answer these questions: connected components, the weak points that
hold a network together, measures of connectivity and minimum cuts, network flows, spanning trees,
and simulations of how networks break apart under failure and attack.

Many of the methods below return edge IDs. A small helper shows those edges with their endpoints'
labels, which makes the results easier to read:

```{python}
import edgecase as ec
import polars as pl


def named_edges(graph, ids=None):
    labels = dict(graph.get_node_df().select("id", "label").iter_rows())
    edges = graph.get_edge_df()
    if ids is not None:
        edges = edges.filter(pl.col("id").is_in(ids))
    return edges.with_columns(
        pl.col("source", "target").replace_strict(labels, return_dtype=pl.String)
    ).drop("rel")
```

## Connected components

A graph is *connected* when there is a path between every pair of its nodes. A disconnected graph
falls into *components*, groups of nodes that can reach one another but nothing outside the group.
[`is_connected()`](../reference/Graph.is_connected.qmd) checks the first, and
[`weakly_connected_components()`](../reference/Graph.weakly_connected_components.qmd) returns the
components as sets of node IDs, largest first. (For undirected graphs the word "weakly" can be
ignored; the distinction matters only for directed graphs, as the next section explains.)

Most real networks consist of one *giant component*, holding most of the nodes, and many small
fragments. The general relativity co-authorship network is typical:

```{python}
coauthors = ec.ca_grqc().simplify()
components = coauthors.weakly_connected_components()

coauthors.is_connected(), len(components), [len(c) for c in components[:5]]
```

Of 5,242 authors, 4,158 belong to one component, and the other 1,084 are spread over 354 small
groups: researchers whose papers were written only with each other. The sizes of the fragments
are easy to tabulate:

```{python}
(
    pl.DataFrame({"size": [len(c) for c in components]})
    .group_by("size")
    .agg(components=pl.len())
    .sort("size")
    .head(6)
)
```

Pairs of authors with a single joint paper are the most common fragment by far. Many measures,
such as distances and closeness, are only meaningful within a component, so it is common to
restrict an analysis to the giant component. [`subgraph()`](../reference/Graph.subgraph.qmd)
extracts it from the list of its node IDs:

```{python}
giant = coauthors.subgraph(list(components[0]))
giant.count_nodes(), giant.is_connected()
```

For a single node, [`node_connected_component()`](../reference/Graph.node_connected_component.qmd)
returns the component it belongs to, and
[`largest_component_size()`](../reference/Graph.largest_component_size.qmd) gives the size of the
giant component without listing it. [`count_weakly_connected_components()`](../reference/Graph.count_weakly_connected_components.qmd)
counts the components, and [`isolates()`](../reference/Graph.isolates.qmd) lists the nodes with no
edges at all, each a component of its own.

### Directed graphs

In a directed graph, edges can only be followed one way, and connectivity comes in two strengths.
A *weakly connected component* is a group of nodes that would be connected if the edge directions
were ignored. A *strongly connected component* is a group in which every node can reach every other
by following the edges forward. The Wikipedia election network, in which an edge runs from each
voter to the candidate they voted on, shows how different the two can be:

```{python}
wiki = ec.wiki_vote()
strong = wiki.strongly_connected_components()

wiki.count_weakly_connected_components(), len(strong), max(len(c) for c in strong)
```

Nearly all of the 7,115 users fall into one weakly connected component, but there are 5,816
strongly connected components. Only 1,300 users form a strongly connected core, in which a chain
of votes leads from any member to any other; most other users are components of their own.

The core organizes the rest of a directed network into what is often called a *bow tie*. The nodes
that can reach the core but can't be reached from it form the *in-component*, and the nodes that
can be reached from it but can't reach it form the *out-component*.
[`ancestors()`](../reference/Graph.ancestors.qmd) and [`descendants()`](../reference/Graph.descendants.qmd)
find both, starting from any member of the core:

```{python}
core = max(strong, key=len)
member = next(iter(core))

in_component = set(wiki.ancestors(member)) - core
out_component = set(wiki.descendants(member)) - core
len(core), len(in_component), len(out_component)
```

The in-component, with 3,858 users, is the largest part: users who voted, directly or through
others, for candidates in the core, but who were never themselves voted on by anyone the core
reaches. The 1,016 users of the out-component received votes from the core but cast none that lead
back into it. The remaining 941 users, in tendrils and isolated pieces, are attached to the bow tie
without passing through its core.

[`condensation()`](../reference/Graph.condensation.qmd) shows the same structure as a graph, by
collapsing each strongly connected component into a single node. The result has no cycles, since a
cycle through several components would make them one component, and each node records its
`members` and `size`:

```{python}
condensed = wiki.condensation()
condensed.count_nodes(), condensed.is_dag()
```

A condensation is the standard way to apply the methods of
[Directed acyclic graphs](17-dags.qmd), such as topological sorting, to a graph with cycles. The
sinks of the condensation, components that no edge leaves, are returned by
[`attracting_components()`](../reference/Graph.attracting_components.qmd). A random walk that
enters one can never leave, which makes them important in the study of Markov chains and of web
crawling. [`is_strongly_connected()`](../reference/Graph.is_strongly_connected.qmd),
[`is_weakly_connected()`](../reference/Graph.is_weakly_connected.qmd), and
[`is_semiconnected()`](../reference/Graph.is_semiconnected.qmd) test a directed graph's overall
connectivity, the last of them checking whether, for every pair of nodes, at least one can reach
the other.

## Weak points

A connected network may still hang together by a thread. A *bridge* is an edge whose removal
disconnects the graph, and an *articulation point*, or cut node, is a node whose removal does.
[`bridges()`](../reference/Graph.bridges.qmd) returns the IDs of the bridge edges and
[`get_articulation_points()`](../reference/Graph.get_articulation_points.qmd) the IDs of the
articulation points:

```{python}
karate = ec.karate_club()
named_edges(karate, karate.bridges()), karate.get_articulation_points()
```

The karate club has one bridge, the only friendship of member `"11"`, and one articulation point,
the instructor (ID 1). Removing the instructor would cut off more than member `"11"`, as the
*biconnected components* show. These are the maximal pieces of a graph that survive the loss of
any one node, and articulation points are the nodes they share.
[`biconnected_components()`](../reference/Graph.biconnected_components.qmd) returns each as a list
of node IDs:

```{python}
[[karate.get_label_from_id(node) for node in block] for block in karate.biconnected_components()]
```

The instructor belongs to all three. Besides the main block of 28 members and the bridge to member
`"11"`, the instructor holds together a small group of five members (`"4"`, `"5"`, `"6"`, `"10"`,
and `"16"`) whose only ties to the rest of the club pass through the instructor.

Infrastructure networks tend to have many such weak points. In the western United States power
grid, a quarter of the lines are bridges and a quarter of the stations are articulation points:

```{python}
grid = ec.power_grid()
blocks = grid.biconnected_components()

(
    grid.count_edges(),
    len(grid.bridges()),
    grid.count_nodes(),
    len(grid.get_articulation_points()),
    max(len(block) for block in blocks),
)
```

Only 3,040 of the 4,941 stations lie in the largest block, the part of the grid that every
station can reach by two independent routes. The rest are attached through branches that a single
failure would cut off. [`has_bridges()`](../reference/Graph.has_bridges.qmd) and
[`is_biconnected()`](../reference/Graph.is_biconnected.qmd) answer the yes-or-no versions of these
questions.

### Local bridges

An edge whose endpoints have no neighbor in common lies on no triangle, and removing it would
lengthen the shortest path between them even if it wouldn't disconnect anything. Such an edge is a
*local bridge*. [`local_bridges()`](../reference/Graph.local_bridges.qmd) returns each one's ID
and *span*, the distance between its endpoints once the edge is removed. In sociology, local
bridges are Granovetter's "weak ties", the links between separate social circles through which new
information tends to arrive:

```{python}
spans = dict(karate.local_bridges())
named_edges(karate, list(spans)).with_columns(
    span=pl.col("id").replace_strict(spans, return_dtype=pl.Float64)
)
```

The true bridge has an infinite span. The other ten local bridges are shortcuts whose removal
would add one step between their endpoints, and seven of them join members of the two factions,
which is just where weak ties should be found.

## Measuring connectivity

How well connected is a network, beyond being connected at all? The *node connectivity* of a graph
is the fewest nodes whose removal disconnects it, and its *edge connectivity* the fewest edges.
By Menger's theorem, the same numbers count independent routes: two nodes that it takes `k` node
removals to separate are joined by `k` paths that share no intermediate node, and the same holds
for edges and edge-disjoint paths (see
[Paths and distances](12-paths.qmd#disjoint-paths)).

For a whole graph, [`get_node_connectivity()`](../reference/Graph.get_node_connectivity.qmd) and
[`get_edge_connectivity()`](../reference/Graph.get_edge_connectivity.qmd) give the two values,
which are also called *cohesion* and *adhesion*
([`get_cohesion()`](../reference/Graph.get_cohesion.qmd) and
[`get_adhesion()`](../reference/Graph.get_adhesion.qmd)). For a single pair of nodes,
[`get_node_connectivity_between()`](../reference/Graph.get_node_connectivity_between.qmd) and
[`get_min_cut_between()`](../reference/Graph.get_min_cut_between.qmd) give the local values, and
[`minimum_node_cut()`](../reference/Graph.minimum_node_cut.qmd) and
[`minimum_edge_cut()`](../reference/Graph.minimum_edge_cut.qmd) return a smallest set that
separates them:

```{python}
(
    karate.get_node_connectivity(),
    karate.get_node_connectivity_between(1, 34),
    karate.minimum_node_cut(1, 34),
    karate.get_min_cut_between(1, 34),
)
```

The whole club has a connectivity of only 1, because of the bridge to member `"11"`. The two
leaders, however, are far better connected than that. It would take the removal of six members, a
set such as the one shown, or of ten friendships, to separate the instructor from the
administrator, and there are six routes between them that share no member.

This illustrates a general point. The connectivity of a whole network is limited by its least
connected node, so in most real networks it is 1 or 2 and says little. The global minimum cut from
[`stoer_wagner()`](../reference/Graph.stoer_wagner.qmd), which finds the lightest set of edges
that splits a graph into two pieces, usually just cuts off a node of the lowest degree:

```{python}
karate.stoer_wagner()
```

Two other tools are more informative. The first looks for the parts of a network that are well
connected internally. [`k_edge_components()`](../reference/Graph.k_edge_components.qmd) splits the
nodes into groups that can't be separated by removing fewer than `k` edges of the graph:

```{python}
[len(group) for group in karate.k_edge_components(4) if len(group) > 1]
```

Sixteen members form the club's 4-edge-connected core, which includes both leaders and their
closest associates; every other member is a group of their own.
[`k_edge_subgraphs()`](../reference/Graph.k_edge_subgraphs.qmd) is the stricter version, in which
the edges used must lie inside each group, and
[`k_components()`](../reference/Graph.k_components.qmd) gives the node-connectivity version for
every `k` at once. The last is the basis of Moody and White's *structural cohesion*, a hierarchy of
ever more cohesive groups. In the Florentine marriage network, ten of the fifteen families form a
2-connected core that survives the loss of any one family:

```{python}
florentine = ec.florentine_families()
{
    k: [[florentine.get_label_from_id(node) for node in group] for group in groups]
    for k, groups in florentine.k_components().items()
}
```

`k_components()` is expensive, since it computes many cuts, and is best kept to graphs with a few
dozen nodes. The cheaper edge-based methods scale much further.

The second tool is the [`gomory_hu_tree()`](../reference/Graph.gomory_hu_tree.qmd), a weighted
tree on the same nodes from which the minimum cut between *any* pair can be read: it is the
lightest edge on the tree path between them. Building the tree costs `n - 1` maximum-flow
computations, after which every one of the `n(n - 1) / 2` pairwise cut values comes free. The
heaviest edges of the tree join the most robustly connected pairs:

```{python}
named_edges(karate.gomory_hu_tree()).sort("weight", descending=True).head(4)
```

The administrator (`"33"`) and member `"32"` are joined by twelve edge-disjoint paths, the most of
any pair, and the instructor and administrator by ten, as found above. The leaders and their
closest allies form the most robustly connected part of the club.
[`all_pairs_node_connectivity()`](../reference/Graph.all_pairs_node_connectivity.qmd) and
[`average_node_connectivity()`](../reference/Graph.average_node_connectivity.qmd) compute the
pairwise node connectivities directly, and [`all_node_cuts()`](../reference/Graph.all_node_cuts.qmd)
lists every smallest set of nodes whose removal disconnects the graph.

### Strengthening a network

The reverse question is a design problem: which links should be added so that a network survives
any `k - 1` link failures? [`k_edge_augmentation()`](../reference/Graph.k_edge_augmentation.qmd)
returns a set of new edges that makes a graph `k`-edge-connected, as pairs of node IDs:

```{python}
karate.k_edge_augmentation(2)
```

One new friendship, between member `"11"` (ID 12) and member `"9"` (ID 10), would leave the karate
club without a bridge. The `avail=` argument restricts the candidates to a list of possible edges,
optionally with a cost for each, such as the cables that could actually be laid and what each
would cost. [`is_k_edge_connected()`](../reference/Graph.is_k_edge_connected.qmd) checks the
result.

## Flows

Connectivity counts routes; *flow* asks how much can travel along them. In a flow network, each
edge has a *capacity*, the most it can carry, and the maximum flow from a source to a sink is the
largest amount that can be sent while respecting every capacity and conserving flow at every node
along the way. The applications include pipelines, traffic and data networks, and many assignment
problems that can be phrased as flows.

The flow methods read each edge's capacity from an edge attribute named `capacity`, or, if there is
none, from its weight on a weighted graph, and otherwise give it a capacity of 1. Here is a small
directed network of pipes:

```{python}
pipes = ec.Graph.from_edges(
    [
        ("s", "a", {"capacity": 16}), ("s", "b", {"capacity": 13}),
        ("b", "a", {"capacity": 4}), ("a", "c", {"capacity": 12}),
        ("c", "b", {"capacity": 9}), ("b", "d", {"capacity": 14}),
        ("d", "c", {"capacity": 7}), ("c", "t", {"capacity": 20}),
        ("d", "t", {"capacity": 4}),
    ],
    directed=True,
)
pipes.max_flow_value("s", "t")
```

[`max_flow_value()`](../reference/Graph.max_flow_value.qmd) gives the total, and
[`max_flow()`](../reference/Graph.max_flow.qmd) returns how much each edge carries, as a dictionary
from edge IDs to amounts. Edges that carry nothing are left out:

```{python}
flows = pipes.max_flow("s", "t")
named_edges(pipes).with_columns(
    flow=pl.col("id").replace_strict(flows, default=0.0, return_dtype=pl.Float64)
)
```

Twenty-three units reach `t`, but the pipes out of `s` could carry 29. The limit lies elsewhere,
and the *max-flow min-cut theorem* says where: the maximum flow equals the capacity of the
narrowest *cut*, the set of edges leading from one side of a division of the nodes to the other.
[`minimum_cut()`](../reference/Graph.minimum_cut.qmd) returns its value and the two sides:

```{python}
value, (source_side, sink_side) = pipes.minimum_cut("s", "t")
value, [pipes.get_label_from_id(node) for node in sink_side]
```

The bottleneck is the three pipes that lead into `c` and `t` from the source side: `a` to `c`
(12), `d` to `c` (7), and `d` to `t` (4), which together carry exactly 23 units, all of them full.
Widening any other pipe would not increase the flow.

Note that [`get_min_cut_between()`](../reference/Graph.get_min_cut_between.qmd) and
[`minimum_edge_cut()`](../reference/Graph.minimum_edge_cut.qmd), from the previous section, count
edges by default, and use capacities only when you name the attribute with `capacity=`.
`max_flow()`, `max_flow_value()`, and `minimum_cut()` use the `capacity` attribute automatically:

```{python}
pipes.get_min_cut_between("s", "t"), pipes.get_min_cut_between("s", "t", capacity="capacity")
```

### The cheapest flow

When edges also have a cost per unit of flow, the question becomes how to send a given amount as
cheaply as possible. [`min_cost_flow()`](../reference/Graph.min_cost_flow.qmd) reads costs from a
`cost` attribute and returns the amount sent, its total cost, and the flow on each edge. Consider a
plant that ships goods to a market through two warehouses, with a link between the warehouses:

```{python}
shipping = ec.Graph.from_edges(
    [
        ("plant", "north", {"capacity": 15, "cost": 4}),
        ("plant", "south", {"capacity": 10, "cost": 2}),
        ("south", "north", {"capacity": 5, "cost": 1}),
        ("north", "market", {"capacity": 12, "cost": 2}),
        ("south", "market", {"capacity": 8, "cost": 5}),
    ],
    directed=True,
)
sent, cost, flows = shipping.min_cost_flow("plant", "market", demand=15)
sent, cost
```

Shipping 15 units costs 88. The edge flows show the solution:

```{python}
named_edges(shipping).with_columns(
    flow=pl.col("id").replace_strict(flows, default=0.0, return_dtype=pl.Float64)
)
```

The cheapest route, through the south warehouse and across to the north (2 + 1 + 2 = 5 per unit),
is used to its limit of five units. The direct route through the north warehouse, at 6 per unit,
takes the next seven, until the link from north to market is full, and the last three units go by
the most expensive route, through the south warehouse directly. Without `demand=`, the method
sends as much as the network can carry, and finds the cheapest way of doing so.

## Spanning trees

A *spanning tree* of a connected graph is a tree that includes all of its nodes: the smallest set
of edges that keeps everything connected. With edge weights, the *minimum spanning tree* is the
lightest such tree, the cheapest way to connect every node. It answers design questions such as
which roads to pave, or along which routes to lay cable, so that every town is served at the least
total cost.

The road network from [Paths and distances](12-paths.qmd) is a good example. Each road's weight is
its length in kilometers, and each city has a `pos` attribute for drawing it as a map:

```{python}
cities = {
    "Amsterdam": (52.37, 4.90), "Brussels": (50.85, 4.35), "Paris": (48.86, 2.35),
    "Lyon": (45.76, 4.84), "Marseille": (43.30, 5.37), "Geneva": (46.20, 6.14),
    "Zurich": (47.37, 8.54), "Milan": (45.46, 9.19), "Munich": (48.14, 11.58),
    "Frankfurt": (50.11, 8.68), "Cologne": (50.94, 6.96), "Berlin": (52.52, 13.40),
    "Prague": (50.08, 14.44), "Vienna": (48.21, 16.37),
}

roads = [
    ("Amsterdam", "Brussels", 210), ("Amsterdam", "Cologne", 260), ("Amsterdam", "Berlin", 655),
    ("Brussels", "Paris", 300), ("Brussels", "Cologne", 210), ("Paris", "Lyon", 465),
    ("Paris", "Frankfurt", 570), ("Lyon", "Marseille", 315), ("Lyon", "Geneva", 150),
    ("Geneva", "Zurich", 280), ("Geneva", "Milan", 320), ("Marseille", "Milan", 600),
    ("Zurich", "Milan", 280), ("Zurich", "Munich", 315), ("Zurich", "Frankfurt", 410),
    ("Cologne", "Frankfurt", 190), ("Frankfurt", "Munich", 390), ("Frankfurt", "Berlin", 545),
    ("Berlin", "Prague", 350), ("Munich", "Prague", 380), ("Munich", "Vienna", 435),
    ("Prague", "Vienna", 330), ("Munich", "Milan", 490),
]

places = [(city, {"pos": [lon, lat]}) for city, (lat, lon) in cities.items()]
road_net = ec.Graph.from_edges(roads, nodes=places, graph_name="Roads")
```

[`minimum_spanning_tree()`](../reference/Graph.minimum_spanning_tree.qmd) returns the tree as a new
graph, with the same nodes and the edges it keeps. Storing each road's length as an attribute lets
the drawing label the roads:

```{python}
tree = road_net.minimum_spanning_tree()
tree.set_edge_attrs("km", {e["id"]: int(e["weight"]) for e in tree.get_edge_df().iter_rows(named=True)})
tree.plot(layout="pos", label_by="label", edge_label_by="km", node_size=10, height=480)
```

The tree uses 13 of the 23 roads, one fewer than the number of cities, and their total length is
3,700 km:

```{python}
tree.count_edges(), tree.get_edge_df()["weight"].sum()
```

A minimum spanning tree is cheap but fragile, since every one of its edges is a bridge, and it can
make journeys much longer. Amsterdam to Berlin is a direct road of 655 km, but in the tree the
route runs south to Munich and back north through Prague:

```{python}
road_net.shortest_path_length("Amsterdam", "Berlin"), tree.shortest_path_length("Amsterdam", "Berlin")
```

The options of
`minimum_spanning_tree()` adapt it to other uses. `include=` and `exclude=` force particular edges
in or out of the tree, `weight_attr=` names another attribute to minimize, and
`return_subgraph=False` returns the IDs of the tree's edges instead of a graph.

The other spanning-tree methods are these:

| Method | Returns |
|---|---|
| [`maximum_spanning_tree()`](../reference/Graph.maximum_spanning_tree.qmd) | the heaviest spanning tree, for example the strongest ties that connect a weighted social network |
| [`number_of_spanning_trees()`](../reference/Graph.number_of_spanning_trees.qmd) | the number of spanning trees, by Kirchhoff's matrix-tree theorem |
| [`random_spanning_tree()`](../reference/Graph.random_spanning_tree.qmd) | a spanning tree drawn at random, with probability proportional to the product of its weights |
| [`iter_spanning_trees()`](../reference/Graph.iter_spanning_trees.qmd), [`all_spanning_trees()`](../reference/Graph.all_spanning_trees.qmd) | spanning trees in order of total weight, or all of them |
| [`minimum_spanning_arborescence()`](../reference/Graph.minimum_spanning_arborescence.qmd), [`maximum_spanning_arborescence()`](../reference/Graph.maximum_spanning_arborescence.qmd) | the directed counterparts: trees with every edge pointing away from a root |

The number of spanning trees measures how many different ways a network can be connected, and so
how much redundancy it has. On a weighted graph, `number_of_spanning_trees()` sums the products of
the weights instead, so pass `weighted=False` to count them:

```{python}
road_net.number_of_spanning_trees(weighted=False)
```

## Algebraic connectivity

A spectral measure gives a finer reading of how well connected a graph is. The *algebraic
connectivity*, from [`algebraic_connectivity()`](../reference/Graph.algebraic_connectivity.qmd), is
the second-smallest eigenvalue of the graph's Laplacian matrix. It is 0 exactly when a graph is
disconnected, and grows with how hard the graph is to cut into two large pieces: a network with a
narrow bottleneck, or one that is long and thin, has a value near 0.

```{python}
networks = {
    "roads": road_net,
    "karate club": karate,
    "dolphins": ec.dolphins(),
    "power grid": grid,
}
{name: round(graph.algebraic_connectivity(weighted=False), 4) for name, graph in networks.items()}
```

The power grid's value is tiny, as befits a network spread across half a continent, and the
dolphins, which live in two loosely linked groups, score well below the karate club. The weights
of the road network are left out with `weighted=False`, since with lengths as weights a larger
value would mean longer roads. The eigenvector that belongs to this eigenvalue, the *Fiedler
vector* ([`fiedler_vector()`](../reference/Graph.fiedler_vector.qmd)), points to where the cut
would fall, and [`spectral_bisection()`](../reference/Graph.spectral_bisection.qmd) uses it to
split a graph in two (see [Communities](14-communities.qmd)).

## Robustness

How does a network degrade as its nodes fail? [`network_robustness()`](../reference/Graph.network_robustness.qmd)
removes nodes one at a time and records the share of the original nodes that remain in the largest
component. The `strategy=` argument sets the order: `"random"` models accidental failures, while
`"degree"` and `"betweenness"` model a targeted attack on the most connected or most central
nodes first. With `return_dict=True` it returns the curve as a list of
`(fraction_removed, largest_component_fraction)` pairs.

A famous result of network science is that networks with hubs, such as the Internet, are robust
to random failure but fragile under attack. Comparing the Internet's autonomous systems with a
random graph of the same size, from [`add_gnm_graph()`](../reference/Graph.add_gnm_graph.qmd),
shows it:

```{python}
internet = ec.internet().simplify()
random_net = ec.Graph().add_gnm_graph(internet.count_nodes(), internet.count_edges(), seed=1)

rows = []
for name, graph in {"Internet": internet, "random graph": random_net}.items():
    n = graph.count_nodes()
    for strategy in ["random", "degree"]:
        curve = graph.network_robustness(strategy=strategy, steps=n // 10, seed=1, return_dict=True)
        rows.append(
            {"network": name, "strategy": strategy}
            | {f"{share:.0%} removed": round(curve[round(share * n)][1], 3) for share in [0.01, 0.02, 0.05, 0.1]}
        )
pl.DataFrame(rows)
```

When nodes fail at random, the two networks behave alike: losing a tenth of the nodes costs the
giant component little more than those nodes themselves. A targeted attack makes no difference to
the random graph, whose nodes all have similar degrees, but it devastates the Internet. Removing
the best-connected 1% of autonomous systems halves its giant component, and removing 5% shatters
it, because nearly every route passes through the hubs. The `steps=` argument stops the simulation
early, which saves time on large graphs when only the first removals are of interest.

[`percolation_threshold_analysis()`](../reference/Graph.percolation_threshold_analysis.qmd) studies
random failure more systematically. For a series of removal fractions it removes nodes at random,
repeats each removal `trials=` times, and averages the share of the *surviving* nodes that remain
in the largest component:

```{python}
{
    name: [round(share, 2) for _, share in graph.percolation_threshold_analysis(steps=5, trials=5, seed=1)]
    for name, graph in {"power grid": grid, "Internet": internet}.items()
}
```

The values are for 0%, 20%, 40%, 60%, 80%, and 100% of the nodes removed. The power grid has few
redundant routes, and once two fifths of its stations have failed, the survivors are scattered in
small fragments. The Internet keeps half of its survivors together even with 60% of its nodes
gone. [`node_percolation()`](../reference/Graph.node_percolation.qmd) and
[`edge_percolation()`](../reference/Graph.edge_percolation.qmd) perform a single round of random
removal and return the surviving graph, for experiments of your own. The spread of epidemics over
networks, which is closely related to percolation, is covered in
[Spreading and robustness](32-spreading.qmd).

## Choosing a method

| Question | Methods |
|---|---|
| Is the graph in one piece, and if not, what are the pieces? | `is_connected()`, `weakly_connected_components()`, `strongly_connected_components()`, `subgraph()` |
| Which single node or edge would disconnect it? | `get_articulation_points()`, `bridges()`, `biconnected_components()` |
| How many independent routes join two nodes? | `get_node_connectivity_between()`, `get_min_cut_between()`, `node_disjoint_paths()` |
| Which parts are robustly connected? | `k_edge_components()`, `k_components()`, `gomory_hu_tree()` |
| How much can flow from one node to another, and where is the bottleneck? | `max_flow()`, `minimum_cut()`, `min_cost_flow()` |
| What is the cheapest way to connect everything? | `minimum_spanning_tree()` |
| How does the network degrade under failure or attack? | `network_robustness()`, `percolation_threshold_analysis()` |
